{{ElectionsAK}}
The '''2026 Alaska gubernatorial election''' is scheduled to take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the next [[Governor of Alaska|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Alaska|lieutenant governor of Alaska]]. A nonpartisan [[top-four primary]] election occurred on August 18, 2026, in which four candidates would advance to a [[Ranked-choice voting in the United States|ranked-choice]] general election.<ref>{{cite web|title = Primary Election Information|url = https://www.elections.alaska.gov/Core/primaryelectioninformation.php|website = Alaska Division of Elections|access-date = 2024-12-15|quote = Primary elections are held on the third Tuesday in August of even numbered years.|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20220504030110/https://www.elections.alaska.gov/Core/primaryelectioninformation.php|archive-date = May 4, 2022|url-status = dead}}</ref> Incumbent governor [[Mike Dunleavy (politician)|Mike Dunleavy]] is term-limited and ineligible to seek a third consecutive term.

==Primary election==

===Campaign===
The primary featured a crowded field of 17 candidates. Candidates at times struggled to distinguish themselves, while Alaska's [[Nonpartisan primary#Alaska|nonpartisan primary]] and [[Ranked-choice voting in the United States#Alaska, 2022–present|ranked-choice voting]] system were credited with encouraging more positive campaigning. As a result, candidates often emphasized areas of agreement, particularly with members of their own party.<ref name="standout">{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |title=In Alaska’s crowded race for governor, candidates struggle to stand out as primary nears |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/08/in-alaskas-crowded-race-for-governor-candidates-struggle-to-stand-out/ |access-date=August 21, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]] |date=August 9, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260810164447/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/08/in-alaskas-crowded-race-for-governor-candidates-struggle-to-stand-out/ |archive-date=August 10, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Republican Bernadette Wilson called on Republican candidates to withdraw if they advanced to the general election but received fewer votes than another Republican, though she was the only candidate to pledge to do so herself. Democrats [[Tom Begich]] and [[Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins]] similarly discussed the possibility of one withdrawing after the primary to consolidate Democratic support behind the other.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Brooks |first1=James |title=After Alaska’s ‘final four’ primary, a silent primary may decide who’s on the ballot in November |url=https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/08/14/after-alaskas-final-four-primary-a-silent-primary-may-decide-whos-on-the-ballot-in-november/ |access-date=August 21, 2026 |work=[[Alaska Beacon]] |date=August 14, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260818213201/https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/08/14/after-alaskas-final-four-primary-a-silent-primary-may-decide-whos-on-the-ballot-in-november/ |archive-date=August 18, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

The race also saw heavy spending. Republicans [[Treg Taylor]] and Matt Heilala, the party's two highest-spending candidates, largely self-funded their campaigns. Heilala contributed $1.4 million to his campaign, while Taylor contributed $600,000. Taylor's contribution violated an Alaska campaign finance deadline, though he argued that the restriction was unconstitutional.<ref name="spending"/> 

Kreiss-Tomkins spent more than any other candidate and reported the largest number of individual Alaskan contributors, although most of his funding came from outside the state, including employees of [[Anthropic]] and others connected to the artificial intelligence industry.<ref name="spending" /><ref name="standout" /> Begich raised approximately $1.2 million, more than half of which came from two wealthy Alaskan donors.<ref name="spending">{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |title=Candidates in Alaska’s open governor’s race spend big ahead of Tuesday’s primary |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/12/candidates-in-alaskas-open-governors-race-spend-big-ahead-of-tuesdays-primary/ |access-date=August 21, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]] |date=August 13, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260814183245/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/12/candidates-in-alaskas-open-governors-race-spend-big-ahead-of-tuesdays-primary/ |archive-date=August 14, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== General election ==
===Campaign===
After initially finishing second in the primary, Begich withdrew and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins, allowing fifth-place finisher Taylor to advance to the general election.<ref name=BegichWithdrawal/> However, the Alaska Public Offices Commission recommended against certifying Taylor's candidacy after finding that his financial disclosure did not substantially comply with state law.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |date=August 28, 2026 |title=Alaska campaign watchdog says Treg Taylor should not be allowed to run for governor |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/28/alaska-campaign-watchdog-says-treg-taylor-should-not-be-allowed-to-run-for-governor/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260829081050/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/28/alaska-campaign-watchdog-says-treg-taylor-should-not-be-allowed-to-run-for-governor/ |archive-date=August 29, 2026 |access-date=August 29, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]]}}</ref> On August 31, [[Lieutenant Governor of Alaska|Lieutenant Governor]] [[Nancy Dahlstrom]] declined to certify Taylor, temporarily elevating his running mate, Candice English, to the gubernatorial nomination; English subsequently selected Taylor's wife, Jodi Taylor, as her running mate.<ref name="Taylor">{{cite web |last=Samuels |first=Iris |date=August 31, 2026 |title=Treg Taylor disqualified from ballot as pressure grows for consolidated governor’s race |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/31/pressure-grows-for-a-consolidated-gop-field-in-alaska-governors-race-as-deadline-nears/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260831200254/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/31/pressure-grows-for-a-consolidated-gop-field-in-alaska-governors-race-as-deadline-nears/ |archive-date=August 31, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]]}}</ref>  On September 4, Dahlstrom reversed her decision and announced that Taylor would be certified after a preliminary review by the Alaska Department of Law raised questions about whether the financial disclosure requirements had been applied consistently.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Samuels |first=Iris |title=Treg Taylor is back in Alaska’s race for governor after election officials reverse decision |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/04/treg-taylor-is-back-in-alaskas-race-for-governor-after-election-officials-reverse-decision/ |access-date=2026-09-05 |website=Anchorage Daily News}}</ref>

In the general election campaign, Taylor softened his messaging and attempted to appeal to independent and Democratic voters. Kreiss-Tomkins pledged that Democrats, Republicans, and independents would be equally represented in his cabinet and emphasized endorsements from [[Moderate Republicans (modern United States)|moderate Republicans]]. In contrast, Wilson criticized [[Bipartisanship in United States politics|bipartisanship]] and said that bipartisan coalitions in the [[Alaska legislature]] had been ineffective.<ref name="Refine">{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |title=Heeding ranked choice voting, candidates refine their strategies in Alaska governor’s race |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/16/heeding-ranked-choice-voting-candidates-refine-their-strategies-in-alaska-governors-race/ |access-date=September 18, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]] |date=September 17, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260917151432/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/16/heeding-ranked-choice-voting-candidates-refine-their-strategies-in-alaska-governors-race/ |archive-date=September 17, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Taylor and Bronson called upon Republican voters to rank all three Republicans in the race, while Wilson urged her supporters not to rank other candidates and renewed her calls for the other Republicans to drop out.<ref name="Refine"/><ref name="WilsonCalls">{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |title=Wilson again calls on her Republican opponents to drop out of Alaska governor’s race |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/18/wilson-again-calls-on-her-republican-opponents-to-drop-out-of-alaska-governors-race/ |access-date=September 19, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]] |date=September 18, 2026}}</ref>

While the three Republican candidates generally agreed on most issues, including opposition to new taxation proposals from Kreiss-Tomkins, Wilson was alone in advocating for a return to paying out full [[Permanent Fund Dividend|Permanent Fund dividends]] according to the statutory formula. Incumbent governor [[Mike Dunleavy (politician)|Mike Dunleavy]] had made a similar promise  during his [[2018 Alaska gubernatorial election|2018]] campaign, but his efforts to implement the proposal had been unsuccessful. In fact, dividends reached a record low during Dunleavy's administration. The other candidates argued that following the statutory formula would be unaffordable for the foreseeable future.<ref name="WilsonCalls"/>

The candidates also diverged on the issue of [[Data center|data centers]]. Bronson and Taylor were generally supportive of data centers, portraying them as an economic opportunity provided they generated their own electricity and did not drive up energy costs. Despite receiving large campaign contributions from donors connected to the artificial intelligence industry, Kreiss-Tomkins advocated for a moratorium on data center construction until a regulatory framework could be developed. He also supported regulation of artificial intelligence more broadly. Wilson also opposed data centers, highlighting their environmental impact and arguing that Kreiss-Tomkins could not be trusted on the issue.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Brooks |first1=James |title=Where do Alaska’s four governor candidates stand on data centers? |url=https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/09/18/where-do-alaskas-four-governor-candidates-stand-on-data-centers/ |access-date=September 21, 2026 |work=[[Alaska Beacon]] |date=September 18, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260920011937/https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/09/18/where-do-alaskas-four-governor-candidates-stand-on-data-centers/ |archive-date=September 20, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
